actionRequired.description:
ACTION REQUIRED:

vendor: Updated `k8s.io/system-validators` to `v1.12.1`. The cgroups validator now throws an error instead of a warning if cgroups v1 is detected on the host and the provided KubeletVersion is `v1.35` or newer.

kubeadm: Started using `k8s.io/system-validators` `v1.12.1` in `kubeadm` `v1.35`. During `kubeadm init`, `kubeadm join`, and `kubeadm upgrade`, the SystemVerification preflight check throws an error if cgroups v1 is detected and the detected `kubelet` version is `v1.35` or newer. For older versions of `kubelet`, a preflight warning is displayed.

To allow cgroups v1 with `kubeadm` and `kubelet` version `v1.35` or newer, you must:
- Ignore the error from the SystemVerification preflight check by `kubeadm`.
- Edit the `kube-system/kubelet-config` ConfigMap and add the `failCgroupV1: false` field before upgrading.
actionRequired.author: neolit123

enrichment.title: cgroup v1 validation now fails for kubelet v1.35+
enrichment.summary: The system‑validators library now treats cgroup v1 as an error (instead of a warning) when the host runs cgroup v1 and the kubelet version is v1.35 or newer. kubeadm’s SystemVerification preflight will fail in this case.
enrichment.action: During upgrade, either bypass the SystemVerification preflight error (e.g., using --ignore-preflight-errors) and modify the kube-system/kubelet-config ConfigMap to set failCgroupV1:false before upgrading, ensuring kubelet can run with cgroup v1 if needed.

issueContext.title: HPA - optimize calculatePodRequestsFromContainers func specific container lookups
issueContext.body:
The `calculatePodRequestsFromContainers` function currently iterates through all containers in a pod, even when a specific container name is provided. This is inefficient. When the container parameter is not an empty string, the function should locate the specified container and return its resource request without iterating through the entire list. We should exit the loop early once the matching container is found.

ref: [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132430/files#r2217338178)

/triage accepted
/assign @laoj2 
/sig autoscaling

enrichment.problem: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler's calculatePodRequestsFromContainers function always iterated over every container in a pod, even when a specific container name was provided, causing unnecessary CPU work and slower scaling decisions for multi‑container pods.
enrichment.affected: Users running the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with container‑specific resource metrics, particularly those with multi‑container pods.
enrichment.fix: The lookup logic now exits as soon as the target container is found, returning its resource request immediately and skipping the remaining containers.
enrichment.impact: Reduces CPU consumption and latency of HPA calculations, leading to faster and more efficient scaling for workloads that rely on per‑container resource metrics, especially in pods with many containers.

issueContext.title: Proposal to Fix nfacct Tests on s390x by Generating Custom Test Data
issueContext.body:
I am working on fixing the nfacct tests for s390x architecture. The issue arises due to the difference in endianness, where the test data is currently structured for little-endian systems, causing failures on s390x (big-endian).
To address this, I propose generating custom test data specifically for s390x by converting little-endian data to big-endian format. This approach ensures the test cases properly validate behavior on big-endian systems.

Currently, I have a sample patch that fixes two test cases:
**valid_with_padding**
**valid_without_padding**

issueContext.title: remove rsync from build
issueContext.body:
There's a _lot_ of complexity in the build system around rsync + build + data containers.

This was mostly added to work around docker desktop filesystem performance on macOS, but also used to support building against docker on a remote VM.

Besides the docker desktop licensing changes probably reducing how many developers are actually using docker desktop, it's not clear that we should still be jumping through this many hoops in the build.

OTOH, removing it may be fairly involved, and it's possible the performance gap is still substantial, even if using filesystem caching (which appears to be replaced now https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/5402).

We should test performance and weigh ripping this stuff out to simplify the build.

cc @thockin @cblecker

/sig release

### What happened?

I am using keda with the prometheus scaler. The query I am using, returns the lag in the message queue i am using, and the threshold is set to `0.1`.

I expected the replica count to stay at the max value. Or alternatively, get an error that we have reached the max value for an external metric value

issueContext.title: NCC-E003660-F9W: Common Certificate Authority Possible for Client CA and Request
issueContext.body:
### NCC-E003660-F9W: Common Certificate Authority Possible for Client CA and Request
Header CA
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
A misconfiguration of the API server could lead to a situation where privilege escalation for
any authenticated user to cluster admin is possible.

**Description**
The Kubernetes API server allows a certificate authority (CA) to be specified (using the `--
client-ca-file flag`) which will be used to verify client certificates under the familiar X.
509 client certificate authentication scheme6. Another CA can be specified (using `--
requestheader-client-ca-file`) that will be used to verify requests authenticated using
the request header scheme (described in the documentation as Authenticating Proxy). If
these two CAs are the same, and the `--requestheader-allowed-names` flag is not used to
specify particular certificate common names that are permitted for request header
authentication, it is possible for any holder of a client certificate from the shared CA to
trivially authenticate to the API server as any user, by using their certificate to authenticate
a request using the request header scheme. While it is not intended that these CAs be the
same, and common Kubernetes deployment methods do not configure the deployment in
this way, it is possible that administrators could be unaware of this pitfall.

The Kubernetes documentation does include some advice against sharing CAs, but is not
explicit about the potentially serious security impact of this specific case.

For an example, please see the original finding on page 18 of the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Repo

enrichment.problem: When the same certificate authority is configured for both --client-ca-file and --requestheader-client-ca-file, and --requestheader-allowed-names is not set, any client certificate can impersonate arbitrary users by using the request header authentication scheme, leading to privilege escalation.
enrichment.affected: Clusters where the API server is configured with overlapping client CA and requestheader client CA without specifying allowed names; any user presenting a client certificate could be exploited.
enrichment.fix: kube-apiserver now enforces that if the two CA files overlap, the --requestheader-allowed-names flag must be provided. The API server will reject configurations that lack this flag, preventing regular client certificates from setting authenticating proxy headers for arbitrary users.
enrichment.impact: Stops a configuration that could let any authenticated user obtain cluster‑admin privileges, strengthening cluster security and preventing unauthorized access.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed a startup probe race condition that caused main containers to remain stuck in "Initializing" state when sidecar containers with startup probes had failed initially but succeeded on restart in pods with `restartPolicy=Never`.

bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Fixed a startup probe race condition that caused main containers to remain stuck in "Initializing" state when sidecar containers with startup probes failed initially but succeeded on restart in pods with restartPolicy=Never.

issueContext.title: main container never starts with restartPolicy: Never and sidecar container has a startupProbe and fails the first attempt
issueContext.body:
### What happened? There is a bug in `kubelet` `startupProbe` if sidecar container is configured. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L249 The worker's decision to continue (return true) or stop (return false) is based only on the pod's restart policy, not the containers (sidecar have restartPolicy:Always) This can lead to a racing condition if the sidecar container fails at the first time and prober incorrectly exits: If sidecar container restarted with no problem at second attempt, startupProbe will never run again. This leads kubelet to think the initContainer never successfully initialized. There is another bug in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober_manager.go#L194 the probe can possibly get recreated here. However if there are more than one containers has startup probes, and the first container has a running probe, it will skip other containers (because of an early`return`). As a result, reproduction requires at least 2 startup probes. With the example in the "How to reproduce", the `main-container` is stuck in Initializing state. kubectl desribe pod
``` $ kubectl describe pod init-probe-bug-repro Name: init-probe-bug-repro Namespace: default Priority: 0 Service Account: default Node: gke-cluster-1-pool-3-7b56b326-2rxq/10.128.0.96 Start Time: Tue, 08 Jul 2025 23:38:27 +0000 Labels: Annotations: Status: Pending IP: 10.112.2.93 IPs: IP: 10.112.2.93 Init Containers: buggy-init-container: Container ID: containerd://5c44b517ecfe0d162a31759d1a7f2399c1954d3d80c3225a0d8bf24d0982e952 Image: busybox Image ID: docker.io/library/busybox@sha256:f85340bf132ae937d2c2a763b8335c9bab35d6e8293f70f606b9c6178

enrichment.problem: When a pod has restartPolicy=Never and includes a sidecar container with a startupProbe that fails on the first attempt but succeeds on restart, the kubelet’s startup probe logic races and never re‑executes the probe. This leaves the main container stuck in the "Initializing" phase, preventing the pod from becoming ready.
enrichment.affected: Users running pods with restartPolicy=Never that include sidecar containers using startup probes; the main containers in those pods were previously blocked in the Initializing state.
enrichment.fix: Adjusted the kubelet startup‑probe handling to consider each container’s probe state rather than only the pod’s restart policy, and fixed probe manager logic so that probes are re‑created and evaluated correctly after a sidecar restart. This eliminates the race condition and allows the main container to proceed once the sidecar’s startup probe succeeds.
enrichment.impact: Pods that rely on sidecar containers with startup probes and use restartPolicy=Never (e.g., batch jobs, one‑shot workloads) will now start correctly instead of remaining indefinitely in Initializing. This restores expected pod lifecycle behavior and prevents silent job failures.

issueContext.title: Confusing use of TooManyRequests error for eviction
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When the Kubernetes API server returns a 429 (throttled), the response may include misleading cause information.

We observed that a pod eviction API call received a response that included _**both**_ of the following fragments:

``` json
"responseStatus": {
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "reason": "TooManyRequests",
  "code": 429
},
```

and

``` json
"responseObject": {
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.",
  "reason": "TooManyRequests",
  "details": {
    "causes": [
      {
        "reason": "DisruptionBudget",
        "message": "The disruption budget [elided] needs 11 healthy pods and has 12 currently"
      }
    ]
  },
  "code": 429
},
```
Note that the `message` given above is confusing, as there are more currently healthy pods than the required number.


### What did you expect to happen?

When a request is rejected due to throttling (429 HTTP response), either
* no other error information should be included; or
* the included error information should indicate throttling

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Provoke a 429 HTTP response and inspect the response. 

### Anything else we need to know?

Issue #88535 seems to be similar - it also describes a 429 response where inclusion of a cause resulted in confusion.

### Kubernetes version

Version: 1.20.9


### Cloud provider

Azure Kubernetes Service

```console
$ uname -a

```

</details>

issueContext.title: AssumeCache may detect the PersistentVolume update later than the scheduler's event handlers
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Let's say we have a scenario where Pod is rejected waiting for a PersistentVolume to be available.
When the PersistentVolume status is updated to `Available`, the scheduler is notified via event handlers.

One of such handlers, in [eventhandling.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L566) is responsible for triggering the Pod's scheduling retry. In this case, the reason is valid, so the Pod is placed in the activeQ (or backoffQ) and then taken to the scheduling.

However, during the (pre)filtering of VolumeBinding plugin, the PersistentVolume objects are [listed](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L825) from the plugin's AssumeCache, which have its own set of the [event handlers](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/util/assumecache/assume_cache.go#L208-L214). If these handlers receive the PV update event later than the main scheduler's handlers, VolumeBinding takes the decision based on an old data, e.g. a PersistentVolume with an old state. As a result, the Pod is [rejected](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L885) and goes back to the scheduling queue.

Ultimately, there won't be any event that would wake up such Pod again, so it will wait indefinitely (precisely, it will be retried by the flushing mechanism that we would like to eventually remove).

issueContext.title: Preemption process does not leave a trait in the scheduler cache causing a race
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

The preemption process that is initiated by the scheduler does not leave the immediate trait in the cache. Due to a race, a pod may come back to the scheduling queue before the in-memory state gets updated (receives a notification about a pod being deleted or marked for deletion DeletionTimestamp != nil) and start the same preemption process again.

Whenever the preemption process identifies a pod eligible for preemption, but learns the pod does no longer exist, it immediately puts the preemptor back to scheduling queue (since it may never receive a notification that wakes it up from the unschedulable queue) and the process repeats in a tight loop, each time producing a pod delete api call.

The factor that triggers this issue is the fact that when a pod being preempted is in the binding process, the scheduler lets it finish the process and IGNORES pod delete notifications, waiting for this async binding process to fail. This creates quite a wide window making the problem very likely to happen in a specific use case, like autoscaling when initial pods jump into nodes they were not intended to and need to be preempted right after). Large number of outgoing api-calls (to delete non-existing pod) generates a big load on the api-server and may generate a snowball effect.

The issue itself exists from a long time, but the PR which closed the loop by activating preemptor pod on failure was added to 1.34 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133213

### What did you expect to happen?

The information about a non-existing pod should be reflected in the in-memory cache to cut that loop.

It could be either recorded right after pod delete was accepted or even better whenever any attempt to delete it failed (non-existing pod)

issueContext.body:
#### What happened

This issue is similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/100467 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/92067.

We have a controller that adds labels to a node after it starts up. It looks like there are cases where the scheduler is able to see the new node labels and schedule a pod, but the kubelet somehow doesn't see the new labels - it has stale data in its informer cache. Whatever the reason for the stale data, the result is that the kubelet rejects the pod with "NodeAffinity failed".

#### What did you expect to happen

Kubelet to be able to detect the new node labels and not reject the pod. 

The only reason that we need to keep the node affinity / node selector check in the kubelet is in case someone sets `nodeName` directly on the pod, so that it does not go through the scheduler, so we can't just remove enforcement on the node level.

The short-term fix would be for the kubelet to synchronously fetch the node object when (and only when) it sees these "NodeAffinity failed" errors and try again. To ensure we do not introduce additional heavy traffic when there many pods being scheduled at once, we will have to keep a new cache, separate from the informer cache. The logic would be like:
- Read the node object from the informer
- If we get a NodeAffinity failed error, read the node object from our new cache
- If we still get a NodeAffinity failed error, fetch the node object synchronously from the api server
The cache should be updated whenever we see a node object that is newer than the one we are currently storing - this can come from either the informer or from the synchronous fetch. 

Long term, maybe we can re-consider the flow for `nodeName`, or leverage something like [kubelet synchronous admission](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O9rDeYhGWMbtg-DQmhqKvNsQSHWJSwvSEeNpXTKMvZg/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.6ggs708p6vvu) to keep the scheduler and kubelet coordinated. There are also some more general discussions ab

enrichment.fix: Kubelet now detects a NodeAffinityFailed condition, checks a fresh node cache, and if needed performs a synchronous fetch of the node object from the API server to get up‑to‑date labels before making the final affinity check.

### What happened?

kubelet plugin API does not support ShareID information. The ShareID is an additional identifier to the device name which may be generated by DRAConsumableCapacity feature ( that is introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5104). 

The DRA driver which refers to this API for preparing resource needs to pass ShareID to CDI spec's device ID. Otherwise, the same node will fail to create a container according to the duplicate ID. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Pods can be successfully created when sharing the same device with DRAConsumableCapacity.

Enable DRAConsumableCapacity feature, Enable DRA driver with allowMultipleAllocations device, Create two pods allocating the same device.

From 
```go
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
to
```go
type DRADevice struct {
	drapbv1.Device
	shareID *types.UID
}
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
implemented code: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/939b1fdd3e3efec3a3c7ea758c394c5aabdfa422

issueContext.title: APF significantly under-reporting seats for watches without RV
issueContext.body: From a recent study, we observed API server’s CPU usage (on a 96 vCPU instance) vs "current_executing_seats" was extremely skewed: Computing the CPU usage/seat during that time, it swings quite a bit (0.4-2.0): For that period in the middle where CPU usage/seat is relatively high, majority of the seat usage comes from "workload-low" priority level: Dissecting it further, we can correlate the usage to watch calls from a particular client: These were all watches with RV unset (could've also been RV set to 0): Such calls are expensive upfront due to initial "Add" events being generated for the entire collection, as required by our [API semantics](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#semantics-for-watch). **So why do they have such low seat usage?** The API server's seat calculation logic intends to count watch calls that don't need to send init events at the lowest cost. It does this by checking SendInitialEvents parameter isn't set to true ([xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8471a6f5b00e93409422f1a39e4655651c105a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/request/list_work_estimator.go#L91-L95)). But that misses the RV unset/0 cases (i.e. legacy watches), under reporting their penalty too. We need to exclude those from incorrectly being assigned minimum seats.

enrichment.problem: Legacy watch requests with ResourceVersion unset or set to 0 generate a large initial list of Add events, but the API Priority and Fairness (APF) seat accounting treated them as cheap. issueContext.title: Overaggressive Routes Controller
issueContext.body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:
/kind bug

**What happened**:
`Route controller` is unnecessary too aggressive. The [current control loop](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/route/route_controller.go#L115) loops through the node list every `10s`. Each node will generate a `GET` call to cloud resource manager (ARM in case of `azure`) to assert the route existence, This quickly burns through the quota afforded to each subscription (the umbrella concept used by `azure` to manage multiple clusters/ resource groups) by the underlaying cloud. Nodes does not change their own ip that frequent on `azure` or any cloud/om-prem deployment for that matter. Once the cluster burns through the quota its control plane will become practically unusable until quota refill, refresh or manual shutdown/start of controller to slow down the calls.

Setting it to higher period is not the best solution, since we need the route controller to kick in in case of scale up/down or the unlikely case of node changing IPs. 

**What you expected to happen**:
`Route Controller` must generate the smallest possible of cloud calls. Ideally, only when needed. And must be reasonably fast in reaction to changing state such as `new nodes`, `deleted nodes`, or changing `node ip`  

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Either run many small clusters (10 X 20 nodes) in the same `azure` subscription (or the equivalent concept on different environments), Or run one large cluster (400++ node). The controller will quickly log `HTTP 429` (in `azure` case) throttling errors 

**Proposed Solution**
change `Route Controller` implementation to `Service Controller` [like](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/service/service_controller.go#L136) implementation using `shared informer`. Because `node` object gets frequently updated (example node status updates) the controller should maintain an in memory c

enrichment.problem: The route controller in the cloud-controller-manager polls the node list every 10 seconds and makes a GET request to the cloud provider for each node to verify route existence. This aggressive polling quickly exhausts cloud API quotas (e.g., Azure ARM quota) when many clusters or nodes share a subscription, leading to control‑plane impairment or outage.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running the cloud‑controller‑manager on Azure (or any cloud provider) that use the route controller, especially those with many nodes or multiple clusters sharing a subscription.
enrichment.fix: Introduced the CloudControllerManagerWatchBasedRoutesReconciliation feature gate. When enabled, the route controller switches from periodic polling to a watch‑based reconciliation model, issuing cloud API calls only on relevant events (node add/delete or IP change), dramatically lowering the number of calls.
enrichment.impact: Reduces unnecessary cloud API traffic, prevents quota exhaustion, and improves stability of clusters that run on Azure (and other clouds) with multiple nodes or clusters per subscription. Operators can enable the gate to restore normal control‑plane operation without sacrificing responsiveness to node changes.

feature.description:

feature.author: neolit123

ACTION REQUIRED

vendor: updated k8s.io/system-validators to v1.12.1. The cgroups validator will now throw an error instead of a warning if cgroups v1 is detected on the host and the provided KubeletVersion is 1.35 or newer.

kubeadm: started using k8s.io/system-validators v1.12.1 in kubeadm 1.35. During `kubeadm init`, `kubeadm join` and `kubeadm upgrade`, the SystemVerification preflight check will throw an error if cgroups v1 is detected and if the detected kubelet version is 1.35 or newer. In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/127172, we decided to emit an event only when a resize is completed. We now want to also emit an event when a resize is marked as pending (deferred or infeasible).

When a deferred resize is retried, we will emit a new event if the message changes (i.e. the node's allocated resources have changed). 

/assign
/sig node
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

enrichment.affected: Clusters using InPlacePodVerticalScaling (vertical pod autoscaling) where pods may be resized in‑place; operators monitoring pod events.

feature.description: kubeadm: Added the `HTTPEndpoints` field to `ClusterConfiguration.Etcd.ExternalEtcd` to configure HTTP endpoints for etcd communication in v1beta4. This separates HTTP traffic (e.g., `/metrics`, `/health`) from gRPC traffic, improving access control. Mirrors etcd’s `--listen-client-http-urls` behavior; if not set, the `Endpoints` field handles both traffic types.
feature.author: SataQiu
feature.userFacingChange: kubeadm: Add `HTTPEndpoints` field to `ClusterConfiguration.Etcd.ExternalEtcd` that can be used to configure the HTTP endpoints for etcd communication in v1beta4. This field is used to separate the HTTP traffic (such as /metrics and /health endpoints) from the gRPC traffic handled by Endpoints. This separation allows for better access control, as HTTP endpoints can be exposed without exposing the primary gRPC interface. Corresponds to etcd's `--listen-client-http-urls` configuration. If not provided, Endpoints will be used for both gRPC and HTTP traffic.

enrichment.problem: kubeadm could only configure a single set of endpoints for external etcd, meaning both gRPC (client) traffic and HTTP traffic (e.g., /metrics, /health) shared the same listeners. enrichment.affected: Clusters that use kubeadm to configure an external etcd cluster and need separate exposure of HTTP endpoints for monitoring or health checks.
enrichment.fix: Introduced a new `HTTPEndpoints` field in `ClusterConfiguration.Etcd.ExternalEtcd` (v1beta4). This field lets users specify separate HTTP URLs for etcd, mirroring etcd’s `--listen-client-http-urls`. When set, HTTP traffic (metrics, health checks) is routed to these endpoints, while the existing `Endpoints` field continues to handle gRPC traffic. If omitted, the previous behavior is preserved.
enrichment.impact: Operators can now expose etcd’s HTTP endpoints for observability or health checks without exposing the gRPC client interface, enabling tighter network policies and improved security posture. It also aligns kubeadm configuration with native etcd options, simplifying setup of external etcd clusters.

feature.author: natasha41575
feature.userFacingChange: Promote InPlacePodVerticalScaling to GA.

enrichment.problem: InPlacePodVerticalScaling was only available as an alpha/beta feature, lacking a stable GA API and guarantees, limiting production use for workloads needing live vertical scaling of pods.
enrichment.affected: Any workloads that require live vertical scaling of pods (e.g., stateful applications, batch jobs) and clusters that want a stable API for this capability.
enrichment.fix: Promoted InPlacePodVerticalScaling to GA, stabilizing the API, making the feature generally available, and cementing its behavior across apiserver, scheduler, and kubelet.
enrichment.impact: Users can now safely use in‑place vertical pod scaling in production, avoiding pod restarts and improving resource elasticity for workloads that need to adjust CPU/memory on the fly.

feature.description: Added `kubectl kuberc view` and `kubectl kuberc set` commands to perform operations against the `kuberc` file.
feature.author: ardaguclu
feature.userFacingChange: Adding new kuberc view/set commands in kubectl to perform operations against kuberc file

enrichment.problem: Users had no built‑in kubectl commands to inspect or modify the kuberc configuration file, requiring manual editing and making it difficult to manage per‑cluster settings.
enrichment.affected: Anyone using kubectl who relies on the kuberc file for cluster‑specific configuration (e.g., developers, CI/CD scripts).
enrichment.fix: Introduces two new subcommands – `kubectl kuberc view` to display the current kuberc file and `kubectl kuberc set` to update entries – enabling safe, command‑line operations on the file.
enrichment.impact: Provides a standard, validated way to work with the kuberc file, reducing errors from manual edits and streamlining configuration management for developers and CI pipelines.

feature.description: The scheduler now clears the `nominatedNodeName` field for Pods upon scheduling or binding failure. External components, such as Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter, should not overwrite this field.
feature.author: ania-borowiec
feature.userFacingChange: The scheduler clears the `nominatedNodeName` field for Pods upon scheduling or binding failure. External components, such as Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter, should not overwrite this field.

enrichment.problem: When a Pod fails to be scheduled or bound, its `nominatedNodeName` field was left unchanged. External controllers (e.g., Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter) could read this stale nomination and make incorrect scaling decisions.
enrichment.affected: Pods that experience scheduling or binding failures, especially in clusters using autoscaling components like Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter.
enrichment.fix: The kube‑scheduler now clears the `nominatedNodeName` field on any scheduling or binding failure, ensuring the field only reflects a current nomination.
enrichment.impact: External autoscaling components will no longer act on outdated nominations, preventing unnecessary node provisioning and reducing scheduling loops or wasted resources.

feature.description: Selected a single device class deterministically when multiple device classes were available for an extended resource.
feature.author: yliaog
feature.userFacingChange: pick one device class deterministically for extended resource when there are more than one

enrichment.problem: When an extended resource advertised multiple device classes, the scheduler could choose any class nondeterministically, leading to unpredictable pod placement and resource allocation.
enrichment.affected: Workloads that request extended resources via device plugins where multiple device classes are advertised; clusters using such device plugins.
enrichment.fix: The scheduler now deterministically selects a single device class (e.g., using a stable ordering) when more than one class is available for an extended resource.
enrichment.impact: Pods that request extended resources with multiple device classes will be scheduled consistently, reducing scheduling variance and potential resource contention.

feature.description: Promoted the `KubeletCrashLoopBackOffMax` feature gate to beta and enabled it by default.
feature.author: hankfreund
feature.userFacingChange: Promoted the `KubeletCrashLoopBackOffMax` feature gate to beta, it is now enabled by default.

enrichment.problem: The kubelet's CrashLoopBackOff backoff could increase without a configured maximum, causing pods that crash repeatedly to wait increasingly long before being restarted, which could delay recovery of failing workloads.
enrichment.affected: All nodes running the kubelet, particularly workloads with pods that experience repeated crashes.
enrichment.fix: Promoted the KubeletCrashLoopBackOffMax feature gate to beta and enabled it by default, introducing a configurable upper bound on the CrashLoopBackOff backoff interval for kubelet-managed pods.
enrichment.impact: Clusters now have a sensible default limit on crash-loop backoff, reducing the maximum wait time before a pod is retried. This improves workload resiliency and reduces operator intervention for pods stuck in long back‑off periods.

feature.description: After fixing regressions detected in `v1.34`, the `SchedulerAsyncAPICalls` feature gate was re-enabled by default.
feature.author: macsko
feature.userFacingChange: The SchedulerAsyncAPICalls feature gate has been re-enabled by default after fixing regressions detected in v1.34.

enrichment.problem: Regressions introduced in v1.34 caused the SchedulerAsyncAPICalls feature gate to be disabled by default, preventing clusters from using the async scheduler API calls.
enrichment.affected: Clusters upgraded to v1.34 where the SchedulerAsyncAPICalls feature gate was disabled, affecting scheduling behavior.
enrichment.fix: The regressions were fixed and the SchedulerAsyncAPICalls feature gate is now re-enabled by default.
enrichment.impact: Clusters upgraded to v1.34 will again have async scheduler API calls enabled, restoring expected scheduling performance and behavior for workloads that rely on this feature.

feature.description: Graduated the fine-grained supplemental groups policy (KEP-3619) to GA.
feature.author: everpeace
feature.userFacingChange: KEP-3619: fined-grained supplemental groups policy is graduated to GA.

enrichment.problem: Before this change, the fine‑grained supplemental groups policy was only available as an alpha/beta feature, requiring feature flags and lacking default, stable support. Clusters that needed precise control over which supplemental group IDs pods could run with had to rely on unstable APIs or custom admission control, increasing complexity and risk of misconfiguration.
enrichment.affected: Any workload that sets or depends on supplemental group IDs in its security context, and administrators who want to enforce fine‑grained group restrictions, are now impacted. The change is transparent for workloads that do not use the policy.
enrichment.fix: Graduates the supplemental groups policy (KEP‑3619) to GA. The policy is now enabled by default without feature gates, with full validation in the API server and enforcement in the kubelet, providing a stable, documented way to restrict or allow specific supplemental group IDs for pods.
enrichment.impact: Cluster administrators can now reliably use the supplemental groups policy to harden pod security without experimental feature flags. This simplifies pod security configuration, reduces the chance of accidental privilege escalation, and ensures consistent behavior across Kubernetes versions.

feature.description: Added configurable per-device health check timeouts to the DRA health monitoring API.
feature.author: harche

enrichment.problem: The DRA health monitoring API used a fixed health‑check timeout for all devices, which could delay detection of unhealthy devices or cause premature failures in diverse device environments.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using the Device Resource Allocation (DRA) feature and device plugins that rely on health monitoring, especially workloads that request specialized devices.
enrichment.fix: Introduced a configurable per‑device health‑check timeout field in the DRA health monitoring API, allowing operators to set appropriate timeout values for each device type.
enrichment.impact: Operators can tune timeout values to match device characteristics, leading to faster and more accurate health reporting, reduced false positives/negatives, and improved workload stability that depends on device resources.

feature.description:

enrichment.affected: All pods scheduled onto nodes that have zone/region labels; workloads that depend on topology labels for spreading, affinity, or custom logic.
enrichment.fix: Graduated the PodTopologyLabelsAdmission admission plugin to Beta and enabled it by default, so pods automatically receive the `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` and `topology.kubernetes.io/region` labels when the assigned node has those labels.

feature.description: Updated the Kubernetes build to use Go `1.25.4`.

feature.description: Graduated the image volume source feature to Beta and enabled it by default.
feature.author: haircommander
feature.userFacingChange: Graduate image volume source to on by default Beta

enrichment.problem: The image volume source (OCI volume) was only available as an alpha feature and disabled by default, requiring users to enable a feature gate to use it.
enrichment.affected: Workloads that need to use image‑based volumes (e.g., Pods using the OCI volume source) and clusters where the feature gate was previously required.
enrichment.fix: The feature has been graduated to beta and is now enabled by default, making the OCI image volume source usable without extra configuration.
enrichment.impact: Users can now mount container images as volumes out‑of‑the‑box, reducing operational overhead and providing a more stable, supported way to use image‑based volumes.

feature.description: Implemented opportunistic batching (KEP-5598) to optimize scheduling for pods with identical scheduling requirements.
feature.author: bwsalmon
feature.userFacingChange: KEP-5598 opportunistic batching is implemented to optimize scheduling for pods that have the same scheduling requirements.

enrichment.problem: When many pods share identical scheduling requirements, the scheduler processes each pod individually, leading to redundant computation, higher latency, and unnecessary CPU usage.
enrichment.affected: Users running large numbers of pods with the same scheduling constraints (affinity, tolerations, node selector, etc.) and the kube-scheduler component itself.
enrichment.fix: Implemented opportunistic batching (KEP-5598) in kube-scheduler, which groups pods with identical requirements and schedules the group together, reducing per‑pod scheduling overhead.
enrichment.impact: Scheduling throughput is increased and latency is reduced for workloads that create many similar pods (e.g., batch jobs, StatefulSets, DaemonSets). This improves overall cluster performance and reduces scheduler load.

enrichment.affected: Anyone who builds Kubernetes from source – including developers, CI pipelines, and downstream distributors – will now use Go 1.25.4 for compilation.

enrichment.impact: All Kubernetes components (kubelet, kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, controller-manager, kubectl, etc.) now benefit from the latest Go runtime security patches, bug fixes, and performance enhancements, improving overall stability and security of clusters.

apiChange.description: Moved the `ImagePullIntent` and `ImagePulledRecord` objects used by the kubelet to track image pulls to the `v1beta1` API version.
apiChange.author: stlaz
apiChange.userFacingChange: The ImagePullIntent and ImagePulledRecord objects used by kubelet to store information about image pulls have been moved to the v1beta1 API version.

enrichment.problem: The ImagePullIntent and ImagePulledRecord objects used by the kubelet to record image pull intentions and results were only available in an internal or older API version, lacking a stable versioned API. This made it difficult to manage, evolve, or interoperate with these objects across Kubernetes upgrades.
enrichment.affected: Kubelet uses these objects to track image pulls; the kube‑apiserver must serve the new v1beta1 resources. Any tooling or controllers that query ImagePullIntent/ImagePulledRecord will need to use the v1beta1 version.
enrichment.fix: The objects have been promoted to the v1beta1 API version, providing a versioned, discoverable API schema for ImagePullIntent and ImagePulledRecord. The kubelet now reads and writes these objects using the v1beta1 version.
enrichment.impact: Cluster operators and kubelet implementations gain a stable, versioned API for tracking image pulls, improving upgrade compatibility and enabling future enhancements or external consumers of these records. It also aligns with the related KEP for ensuring secret‑pulled images.

apiChange.description:
Enabled in-place resizing of pod-level resources.  
- Added `Resources` in `PodStatus` to capture resources set in the pod-level cgroup.  
- Added `AllocatedResources` in `PodStatus` to capture resources requested in the `PodSpec`.
apiChange.author: ndixita
apiChange.userFacingChange:
This change allows In Place Resize of Pod Level Resources 
- Add Resources in PodStatus to capture resources set at pod-level cgroup
- Add AllocatedResources in PodStatus to capture resources requested in the PodSpec

enrichment.problem: Pods could not have their CPU or memory limits/requests changed while running; any change required pod deletion and recreation, limiting dynamic workload scaling.
enrichment.affected: Any running pod whose CPU or memory limits need to be changed, especially workloads that rely on dynamic scaling such as batch jobs, stateful services, or custom autoscalers.
enrichment.fix: Introduced in‑place pod resource resizing by adding `Resources` and `AllocatedResources` fields to `PodStatus`. `Resources` reflects the actual resources applied to the pod’s cgroup, while `AllocatedResources` records the resources requested in the pod spec, enabling the control plane to track and adjust resources without pod restart.
enrichment.impact: Operators can now adjust pod resource limits on the fly, improving flexibility for workloads with variable demand, reducing downtime, and simplifying autoscaling or manual tuning workflows.

apiChange.description: Promoted ReplicaSet and Deployment `.status.terminatingReplicas` tracking to beta. The `DeploymentReplicaSetTerminatingReplicas` feature gate is now enabled by default.
apiChange.author: atiratree

enrichment.problem: The .status.terminatingReplicas field for ReplicaSets and Deployments was only available as an alpha feature and disabled by default, leaving users without visibility into the number of pods that were in the process of terminating during rollouts.
enrichment.affected: Users of Deployments and ReplicaSets who rely on status information for rolling updates and automation were previously unable to see terminating replica counts; now they have accurate status data.
enrichment.fix: Promoted the terminatingReplicas tracking to beta and enabled the DeploymentReplicaSetTerminatingReplicas feature gate by default, adding the .status.terminatingReplicas field to the API for Deployments and ReplicaSets.
enrichment.impact: Operators and automation can now reliably observe and react to the number of terminating pods during rolling updates, improving rollout monitoring, debugging, and custom scaling logic without needing to manually enable a feature gate.

apiChange.description: Promoted HPA configurable tolerance to beta. The `HPAConfigurableTolerance` feature gate has now been enabled by default.
apiChange.author: jm-franc

enrichment.problem: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) configurable tolerance feature was behind a disabled feature gate, requiring users to manually enable it before they could customize scaling tolerance.
enrichment.affected: Users of the HPA who wanted to adjust scaling tolerance were forced to enable a feature gate manually; now all HPA users benefit from the default‑on behavior.
enrichment.fix: The HPAConfigurableTolerance feature gate is promoted to beta and enabled by default, making the configurable tolerance option available out‑of‑the‑box.
enrichment.impact: Operators can now set custom tolerance values for HPA scaling decisions without extra feature‑gate configuration, simplifying deployments and giving finer control over scaling stability.

apiChange.description: Promoted the `MaxUnavailableStatefulSet` feature to beta and enabling it by default.

enrichment.problem: The MaxUnavailableStatefulSet feature was in alpha and disabled by default, requiring users to manually enable the feature gate to get MaxUnavailable behavior for StatefulSet rolling updates.
enrichment.affected: Users of StatefulSets who want MaxUnavailable semantics during rolling updates; clusters that relied on the alpha feature gate.
enrichment.fix: Promoted MaxUnavailableStatefulSet to beta and enabled the feature gate by default, making the MaxUnavailable semantics available for StatefulSets out‑of‑the‑box.
enrichment.impact: Users can now safely perform rolling updates of StatefulSets with MaxUnavailable semantics without extra configuration, benefiting from a more stable and battle‑tested implementation.

apiChange.description: Enabled `kubectl get -o kyaml` by default. To disable it, set `KUBECTL_KYAML=false`.

enrichment.affected: All users of the kubectl CLI, especially those who run `kubectl get` in scripts or automation that depend on the default output format.
enrichment.fix: Enabled the `-o kyaml` output format for `kubectl get` by default. Users can opt out by setting the environment variable `KUBECTL_KYAML=false`.
enrichment.impact: kubectl users get kyaml-formatted results out‑of‑the‑box, simplifying integration with tools that parse kyaml. Existing scripts that relied on the previous default can retain the old behavior by explicitly disabling the feature.

apiChange.description:
Introduced the Node Declared Features capability (alpha), which includes:
- A new `Node.Status.DeclaredFeatures` field for publishing node-specific features.
- A `component-helpers` library for feature registration and inference.
- A `NodeDeclaredFeatures` scheduler plugin to match pods with nodes that provide required features.
- A `NodeDeclaredFeatureValidator` admission plugin to validate pod updates against a node's declared features.
apiChange.author: pravk03
apiChange.userFacingChange:
This change adds a new alpha feature Node Declared Features, which includes:
- A new `Node.Status.DeclaredFeatures` field for Kubelet to publish node-specific features.
- A library in `component-helpers` for feature registration and inference.
- A scheduler plugin (`NodeDeclaredFeatures`) scheduler plugin to match pods with nodes that provide their required features.
- An admission plugin (`NodeDeclaredFeatureValidator`) to validate pod updates against a node's declared features.

enrichment.problem: Kubernetes had no built-in mechanism for nodes to advertise their specific capabilities (e.g., hardware features) and for the scheduler or admission control to ensure pods are placed only on nodes that actually provide those capabilities.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that need to schedule workloads based on node‑specific capabilities (e.g., GPU, NIC, CPU extensions). Cluster admins and developers of such workloads gain a way to declare and enforce required features.
enrichment.fix: Introduced the alpha Node Declared Features feature: a new `Node.Status.DeclaredFeatures` field for Kubelet to publish node capabilities, a `component-helpers` library for registration/inference, a `NodeDeclaredFeatures` scheduler plugin to match pods to nodes offering required features, and a `NodeDeclaredFeatureValidator` admission plugin that validates pod updates against a node's declared features.
enrichment.impact: Allows cluster operators to expose node‑specific features, enables the scheduler to make placement decisions based on those features, and prevents pods from being scheduled onto incompatible nodes, improving reliability for workloads that depend on special hardware or software capabilities.

apiChange.description: Enhanced discovery responses to merge API groups and resources from all peer apiservers when the `UnknownVersionInteroperabilityProxy` feature is enabled.
apiChange.author: richabanker
apiChange.userFacingChange: Enhanced discovery response to support merged API groups/resources from all peer apiservers when UnknownVersionInteroperabilityProxy feature is enabled

enrichment.problem: When the UnknownVersionInteroperabilityProxy feature is enabled, the API server's discovery endpoints only returned the groups and resources of the local apiserver instance. In multi‑apiserver (HA) setups this caused clients to miss API groups/resources that existed on peer apiservers, leading to errors when trying to discover or proxy unknown versions.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running multiple apiserver replicas with the UnknownVersionInteroperabilityProxy feature enabled; any client performing discovery against those apiservers.
enrichment.fix: The discovery response logic is enhanced to merge API groups and resources from all peer apiservers. When the feature flag is on, the apiserver aggregates the discovery information across the HA control‑plane and returns a unified list.
enrichment.impact: Clients and controllers that rely on discovery (e.g., kubectl, client libraries, and the UnknownVersionInteroperabilityProxy) now receive a complete view of the cluster’s API surface, preventing failed lookups and improving reliability of cross‑version proxying in HA clusters.

apiChange.description: Feature gate dependencies are now explicit, and validated at startup. A feature can no longer be enabled if it depends on a disabled feature. In particular, this means that `AllAlpha=true` will no longer work without enabling disabled-by-default beta features that are depended on (either with `AllBeta=true` or explicitly enumerating the disabled dependencies).
apiChange.author: tallclair

issueContext.title: Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies
issueContext.body:
It's becoming increasingly common to add new feature gates for extensions on features that still have a feature gate. Today we handle this in an ad-hoc way, where we sometimes check both feature gates (the one directly controlling the new extension, and the one for the original feature), but in lots of cases we just check the direct feature gate.

Rather than checking multiple feature gates wherever the extension feature is used, I propose:
1. Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies, so if feature B depends on feature A, we make this explicit in the feature gate spec, and validate it on startup
    - Only allow a feature to be enabled if all it's dependent features are also enabled. Enforced in [`featureGate.Validate`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9da4b7ecfb60ea484f8e6c89c42e63506571bc68/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/feature_gate.go#L304).
    - Only allow a feature to graduate, if all it's dependent features are at least the same level of maturity. In other words, if feature A is beta, feature B can graduate to beta, but it cannot graduate to GA. (What does this mean for deprecation?). Enforced in unit test.
3. Wherever we need to check if feature B is enabled, we only check feature B, and rely on the validation to ensure that feature A is also enabled.

For an example, the new `InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132919) depends on _both_ `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` and `PodLevelResources`.

/kind feature
/sig architecture
/cc @JoelSpeed @liggitt @jpbetz @siyuanfoundation

enrichment.problem: Feature gate dependencies were not explicit and were not validated at startup, allowing users to enable a feature without its required dependent features (e.g., enabling AllAlpha=true while its dependent beta features remained disabled). This could lead to unexpected runtime failures or silent misconfigurations.
enrichment.affected: Any Kubernetes component that uses the feature‑gate mechanism and had configurations relying on implicit dependency handling, such as clusters using AllAlpha=true without enabling dependent beta features.
enrichment.fix: Inter‑FeatureGate dependencies are now declared in the feature gate spec and validated during component startup. A feature can only be enabled if all of its dependent features are also enabled, requiring users to enable required beta features via AllBeta=true or by enumerating the dependencies explicitly.
enrichment.impact: Clusters with feature‑gate settings that relied on the previous lax validation (especially those using AllAlpha=true) must update their configuration to enable required dependent features. The change prevents hidden dependency issues and makes feature‑gate configuration predictable and safe.

apiChange.description: Updated storage version for `MutatingAdmissionPolicy` to `v1beta1`.
apiChange.author: cici37
apiChange.userFacingChange: The storage version for MutatingAdmissionPolicy is updated to v1beta1.

issueContext.title: Using beta version for the stored version in 1.35 for MutatingAdmissionPolicy
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

We use alpha as the stored version while promoting to beta for MutatingAdmissionPolicy(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132821#discussion_r2205133754). This issue is to track the stored version update in 1.35.

### Why is this needed?

This issue is to track the stored version update in 1.35.

/assign

enrichment.problem: MutatingAdmissionPolicy was stored in etcd using the alpha version, which is inconsistent with its promoted beta API version and can cause upgrade and compatibility issues.
enrichment.affected: Clusters utilizing MutatingAdmissionPolicy, especially during upgrades to 1.35, may have encountered version mismatches in etcd storage.
enrichment.fix: The stored version for MutatingAdmissionPolicy is updated to v1beta1, aligning the persisted representation with the beta API.
enrichment.impact: Clusters that use MutatingAdmissionPolicy will have a smoother upgrade path to 1.35 and future releases, avoiding data migration complexities and ensuring consistency between the API and stored data.

apiChange.description: Added the `--min-compatibility-version` flag to `kube-apiserver`, `kube-controller-manager`, and `kube-scheduler`.
apiChange.author: siyuanfoundation
apiChange.userFacingChange: Added a new `--min-compatibility-version` command line setting for kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler.

enrichment.problem: Before this change there was no mechanism for the control plane components (kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler) to enforce a minimum API version compatibility, making it difficult to guard against version‑skew issues during upgrades.
enrichment.affected: Cluster operators performing upgrades or managing version skew across control‑plane components. The change affects workloads that interact with the API server, controller manager, or scheduler when version compatibility is enforced.
enrichment.fix: Introduces a new command‑line flag `--min-compatibility-version` for kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, and kube-scheduler. The flag allows administrators to specify the lowest API version that the component will accept, causing the component to reject requests from older versions that could lead to incompatibilities.
enrichment.impact: Improves upgrade safety and operational reliability by enabling explicit version‑skew control. Clusters can now prevent newer API objects from being processed by older control‑plane components, reducing the risk of runtime errors during rolling upgrades.

apiChange.description: DRA device taints: `DeviceTaintRule` status provides information about the rule, including whether Pods still need to be evicted (`EvictionInProgress` condition). The newly added `None` effect can be used to preview what a `DeviceTaintRule` would do if it used the `NoExecute` effect and to taint devices (`device health`) without immediately affecting scheduling or running Pods.
apiChange.author: pohly
apiChange.userFacingChange: DRA device taints: DeviceTaintRule status provided information about the rule, in particular whether pods still need to be evicted ("EvictionInProgress" condition). The new "None" effect can be used to preview what a DeviceTaintRule would do if it used the "NoExecute" effect and to taint devices ("device health") without immediately affecting scheduling or running pods.

enrichment.problem: Cluster administrators could not preview the impact of a DeviceTaintRule with the NoExecute effect, and there was no way to taint a device for health reasons without immediately triggering pod eviction or affecting scheduling.
enrichment.affected: Users of Device Resource Allocation (DRA) device taints – typically cluster admins and workloads that depend on device health taints for scheduling decisions.
enrichment.fix: Introduced a new "None" effect for DeviceTaintRule and added status information (EvictionInProgress condition). The None effect lets users see what would happen with a NoExecute taint without causing eviction, and allows tainting devices for health monitoring without impacting scheduling or running pods.
enrichment.impact: Enables safer device health management and risk‑free testing of taint rules, reducing unexpected pod evictions and giving admins clearer visibility into rule status.

apiChange.description: Updated the Partitionable Devices feature to support referencing counter sets across ResourceSlices within the same resource pool. Devices from incomplete pools were no longer considered for allocation. This change introduced backwards-incompatible updates to the alpha feature, requiring any ResourceSlices using it to be removed before upgrading or downgrading between v1.34 and v1.35.
apiChange.author: mortent
apiChange.userFacingChange:
Updates to the Partitionable Devices feature which allows for referencing counter sets across different ResourceSlices within the same resource pool.

Devices from incomplete pools are no longer considered for allocation.

This contains backwards incompatible changes to the Partitionable Devices alpha feature, so any ResourceSlices that uses the feature should be removed prior to upgrading or downgrading between 1.34 and 1.35.

enrichment.problem: The alpha Partitionable Devices feature could not reference counter sets across ResourceSlices in the same resource pool, and devices from incomplete pools were still considered for allocation, leading to incorrect device assignment. Upgrading between v1.34 and v1.35 required existing ResourceSlices using this feature to be removed due to backward‑incompatible API changes.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that have enabled the Partitionable Devices alpha feature and created ResourceSlices referencing it, especially those upgrading or downgrading between Kubernetes v1.34 and v1.35.
enrichment.fix: Extended the Partitionable Devices implementation to allow counter set references across ResourceSlices within a single pool and excluded devices from incomplete pools from allocation. Added a breaking change to the alpha API, requiring removal of any existing ResourceSlices that use the feature before upgrading or downgrading between v1.34 and v1.35.
enrichment.impact: Ensures correct device allocation by only using devices from fully defined pools, preventing allocation failures or mis‑placement of workloads that depend on partitionable devices. Administrators must delete relevant ResourceSlices before cluster upgrades, avoiding upgrade errors.

apiChange.description:

apiChange.author: yliaog
apiChange.userFacingChange:
ResourceQuota now counts device class requests within a ResourceClaim object as consuming two additional quotas when the DRAExtendedResource feature is enabled:
- `requests.deviceclass.resource.k8s.io/<deviceclass>` with a quantity equal to the worst case count of devices requested
- requests for device classes that map to an extended resource consume `requests.<extended resource name>`

enrichment.problem: ResourceQuota did not account for device class requests made through a ResourceClaim when the DRAExtendedResource feature was enabled, leading to inaccurate quota usage tracking.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using ResourceQuota together with Device Resource Allocation (DRA) and ResourceClaims that request device classes; pod workloads that request such devices.
enrichment.fix: When DRAExtendedResource is enabled, ResourceQuota now counts device class requests within a ResourceClaim as two separate quotas: (1) `requests.deviceclass.resource.k8s.io/<deviceclass>` with a quantity equal to the worst‑case number of devices requested, and (2) for device classes that map to an extended resource, the request also consumes `requests.<extended resource name>`.
enrichment.impact: Quota enforcement for device resources becomes accurate, preventing over‑allocation of devices and ensuring clusters respect defined resource limits for workloads that use DRA.

apiChange.description: Introduced a new declarative validation tag `+k8s:customUnique` to control listmap uniqueness.

enrichment.fix: Added a new declarative validation tag `+k8s:customUnique` that can be applied to listmap fields. The validation generator recognizes the tag and produces runtime checks that ensure each entry in the listmap is unique.
enrichment.impact: CRD authors can now express uniqueness constraints directly in Go struct tags, reducing the need for custom webhook logic and preventing duplicate entries from being persisted. This improves API reliability and developer ergonomics.

apiChange.description: Made node affinity in Persistent Volume mutable.

issueContext.title: Use `secrets` field in `NodePublishVolumeRequest` for sa tokens
issueContext.body:
If the `TokenRequests` field is set in the `CSIDriver` spec, the tokens are generated and funneled from kubelet to driver as part of volume attributes map. The key for the tokens in the map is `csi.storage.k8s.io/serviceAccount.tokens`.  The service account tokens can be used for workload identity in cloud providers. Especially in case of Secrets Store CSI Driver, these service account tokens are used to access external secrets store to get secrets and mount in the volume. 

As these tokens are sensitive information, it doesn't feel right to include these in the volume context map along with pod name, namespace, service account name which are non-sensitive information. There is a dedicated [secrets field in the proto](https://github.com/container-storage-interface/spec/blob/master/lib/go/csi/csi.pb.go#L4063-L4066) which today is being used for `nodePublishSecretRef` that would be more appropriate for tokens.

To provide more context on "why this issue", we had a CVE in the Secrets Store CSI Driver (ref: [CVE-2023-2878](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/secrets-store-csi-driver/security/advisories/GHSA-g82w-58jf-gcxx)) where the service account tokens were logged as part of the GRPC request in the driver. We use the [protosanitizer](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-lib-utils/blob/master/protosanitizer/protosanitizer.go) in the driver to sanitize the requests before logging but given volume context is not really considered a "secret", the tokens were skipped and logged. We got around this by building custom logic for logging in the driver to strip the tokens but this is something every driver would need to do to be careful and not log the tokens. A change could be made in protosanitizer to sanitize this but given volume context is a map, either entire map needs to be marked a secret or sanitizing has to be done on a field by field basis. Although this prompted me to create this issue, I think volume context is not really "secrets" and appropriate field for s

enrichment.problem: CSI drivers received service account tokens via the volume context map, causing sensitive tokens to be logged and potentially exposed (e.g., CVE-2023-2878 in Secrets Store CSI driver).
enrichment.affected: CSI drivers that use TokenRequests (e.g., Secrets Store CSI driver) and the clusters running those drivers, because tokens are no longer exposed in volume attributes.
enrichment.fix: Introduced the `spec.serviceAccountTokenInSecrets` flag on the CSIDriver object. When set to true, kubelet supplies service account tokens in the `secrets` field of the NodePublishVolumeRequest instead of the volume context, preventing token leakage. The behavior is gated by the `CSIServiceAccountTokenSecrets` feature gate (beta in v1.35).
enrichment.impact: Reduces the risk of credential exposure in logs and other outputs, enhancing cluster security for any workloads that rely on CSI drivers for secret access or workload identity.

issueContext.title: Deletion of csi-node-plugin Pod causes driver entry to be removed from CSINode object; kube-scheduler schedules more than driver's allocatable
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

With @plkokanov we hit in our environments the following issue multiple times:
```
% k -n shoot--foo--bar describe po etcd-main-0

Events:
  Type     Reason              Age                 From                     Message
  ----     ------              ----                ----                     -------
  Warning  FailedAttachVolume  35s (x47 over 80m)  attachdetach-controller  AttachVolume.Attach failed for volume "pv-shoot--shik--shak-1234" : rpc error: code = Internal desc = Attach volume /subscriptions/<omitted>/resourceGroups/shoot--shik--shak/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/pv-shoot--shik--shak-1234 to instance shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5 failed with Retriable: false, RetryAfter: 0s, HTTPStatusCode: 409, RawError: {\r
  "error": {\r
    "code": "OperationNotAllowed",\r
    "message": "The maximum number of data disks allowed to be attached to a VM of this size is 16.",\r
    "target": "dataDisks"\r
  }\r
}
```

When we checked, the CSINode object for the corresponding Node was reporting the correct volume attachment limit:
```
% k get csinode shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5 -o yaml

spec:
  drivers:
  # ...
  - allocatable:
      count: 16
    name: disk.csi.azure.com
    nodeID: shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5
    topologyKeys:
    - topology.disk.csi.azure.com/zone
    - topology.kubernetes.io/zone
```

According to the Node status and according to the VM state in Azure, it had already 16 disks attached.
```
% k get no shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5 -o json | jq '.status.volumesAttached | length'
16

% az vm show -g shoot--shik--shak --name shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5 | jq '.storageProfile.dataDisks | length'
16
```

kube-scheduler wrongly sheduled a Pod with a volume to the `shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5` Node as the Node already had its volume attachments limit reached.

We found

enrichment.problem: The scheduler could place Pods on nodes that no longer had the required CSI driver reported in the CSINode object (e.g., after the csi-node-plugin Pod was deleted), leading to volume attach failures because the node’s allocatable limits were still considered available.
enrichment.affected: Pods that require a specific CSI storage driver and nodes where the driver entry was missing from the CSINode object.
enrichment.fix: kube-scheduler now checks that a node’s CSINode entry contains the needed CSI driver before considering the node for scheduling. If the driver is missing, the node is excluded from the candidate list, preventing pods from being scheduled onto nodes that cannot attach the requested volume.
enrichment.impact: Prevents repeated volume attach errors and pod start failures, improving workload reliability and reducing operational friction for clusters that use CSI drivers.

apiChange.description:
- Enabled the `NominatedNodeNameForExpectation` feature in kube-scheduler by default.
- Enabled the `ClearingNominatedNodeNameAfterBinding` feature in kube-apiserver by default.
apiChange.author: ania-borowiec
apiChange.userFacingChange: Features: NominatedNodeNameForExpectation in kube-scheduler and CleaeringNominatedNodeNameAfterBinding in kube-apiserver are now enabled by default.

enrichment.problem: The NominatedNodeName field used by the scheduler for pod expectations and its cleanup after a pod is bound were optional features that were disabled by default. This could lead to stale nomination data and inaccurate scheduling expectations in clusters where the features were not manually enabled.
enrichment.affected: All clusters that use the default Kubernetes control‑plane components. The change primarily affects scheduling behavior and API handling of the NominatedNodeName field.
enrichment.fix: Both the NominatedNodeNameForExpectation feature in kube‑scheduler and the ClearingNominatedNodeNameAfterBinding feature in kube‑apiserver are now enabled by default, ensuring that nomination expectations are recorded and cleared automatically without extra configuration.
enrichment.impact: Clusters now get correct pod‑placement expectations and automatic cleanup of nomination state, improving scheduling accuracy and preventing the buildup of stale nomination information that could affect scheduling decisions.

apiChange.description:
Introduced the alpha `MutableSchedulingDirectivesForSuspendedJobs` feature gate (disabled by default), which allows mutating a Job's scheduling directives while the Job is suspended. 
It also updates the Job controller to clears the `status.startTime` field for suspended Jobs.
apiChange.author: mimowo
apiChange.userFacingChange:
Introduce the alpha MutableSchedulingDirectivesForSuspendedJobs feature gate (disabled by default) which:
1. allows to mutate Job's scheduling directives for suspended Jobs
2. makes the Job controller to clear the status.startTime field for suspended Jobs

enrichment.problem: Jobs could not have their scheduling directives (e.g., node selectors, affinities) changed while the Job was suspended, and the Job controller retained the original status.startTime even after suspension, leading to stale or inaccurate start time information.
enrichment.affected: Users who suspend Jobs and later need to modify scheduling-related fields (node selectors, affinities, resource requests) and rely on accurate Job start time metadata.
enrichment.fix: Introduces the alpha MutableSchedulingDirectivesForSuspendedJobs feature gate (off by default) that allows mutating a Job's scheduling directives while it is suspended and updates the Job controller to clear the status.startTime field for suspended Jobs.
enrichment.impact: Enables users to adjust resource requests, node selection, or other scheduling parameters of a Job without having to delete and recreate it, improving operational flexibility and ensuring start time reflects the actual execution window.

apiChange.description: The `KubeletEnsureSecretPulledImages` feature was promoted to Beta and enabled by default.
apiChange.author: aramase
apiChange.userFacingChange: The KubeletEnsureSecretPulledImages feature is now beta and enabled by default.

enrichment.problem: The KubeletEnsureSecretPulledImages feature was only available as an alpha gate and disabled by default, requiring users to manually enable it to ensure image pull secrets are used when pulling container images.
enrichment.affected: Any cluster using the kubelet to pull container images with associated pull secrets, especially those that previously ran with the feature disabled.
enrichment.fix: The feature has been promoted to beta and is now enabled by default in the kubelet, so image pull secrets are automatically respected without extra configuration.
enrichment.impact: Clusters no longer need to enable a feature gate to correctly handle image pull secrets, reducing configuration complexity and preventing image pull failures for workloads that rely on pull secrets.

documentation.description: Promoted the `--chunk-size` flag to stable. The kubectl `describe`, `get`, `drain`, and `events` commands can use `--chunk-size` flag to set chunk size.
documentation.author: soltysh
documentation.userFacingChange: kubectl describe, get, drain and events have the ability to set chunk-size using --chunk-size flag, which is now officially stable.

deprecation.description: Marked `ipvs` mode in kube-proxy as deprecated, which will be removed in a future version of Kubernetes. Users are encouraged to migrate to `nftables`.
deprecation.author: adrianmoisey
deprecation.userFacingChange: Mark ipvs mode in kube-proxy as deprecated. ipvs mode in kube-proxy is deprecated and will be removed in a future version of Kubernetes. Users are encouraged to move to nftables.

enrichment.problem: The `ipvs` mode for kube-proxy is deprecated and will be removed in a future Kubernetes version, leaving clusters that rely on it without a supported traffic‑distribution backend.
enrichment.affected: Users running kube-proxy with `ipvs` mode (typically on clusters that rely on IPVS for service load balancing).
enrichment.fix: The release marks `ipvs` mode as deprecated, updates documentation and release notes, and advises users to migrate to the supported `nftables` mode for kube-proxy.
enrichment.impact: Clusters using `ipvs` will need to switch to `nftables` before the feature is removed to avoid loss of service load‑balancing. Migrating now ensures continued network traffic distribution and future compatibility.

deprecations.reason: cgroup v2 is the modern standard

enrichment.summary: Support for cgroup v1 is being deprecated in favor of the modern cgroup v2 standard.
enrichment.impact: Node operators must transition nodes to cgroup v2; workloads running on nodes using cgroup v1 may experience failures if the transition is not completed before the deprecation takes effect.
migrationSteps: Verify that the underlying operating system and kernel support cgroup v2.
Update node configuration (e.g., kubelet config) to use cgroupDriver: "systemd" and set the appropriate cgroup version settings.
Reboot nodes to enable cgroup v2, ensuring that the kubelet starts with the cgroupv2 flag or appropriate configuration.
Validate that all workloads operate correctly under cgroup v2 using monitoring and testing.
Remove any legacy cgroup v1 configuration or flags from node and kubelet settings.

enrichment.summary: The ipvs mode in kube‑proxy is being deprecated due to maintenance burden and technical debt, and will be replaced by the nftables mode.
enrichment.impact: Clusters that currently run kube‑proxy in ipvs mode must transition to nftables mode; failure to do so may result in kube‑proxy failing to start or degraded service routing when ipvs support is removed.
migrationSteps: Update the kube-proxy configuration (ConfigMap or command‑line flags) to set mode: "nftables" instead of "ipvs".
Ensure the kernel modules required for nftables are loaded and that the underlying OS supports nftables.
Remove any ipvs‑specific settings or modules from the nodes.
Redeploy or restart kube‑proxy to apply the new configuration.
Validate network routing and service load‑balancing behavior after the switch.

enrichment.summary: Support for containerd 1.x is being deprecated to align with the end‑of‑life of containerd 1.7; users should move to containerd 2.0+.
enrichment.impact: Node operators must upgrade the container runtime; clusters still using containerd 1.x may face node startup failures or lack of support once the deprecation takes effect, potentially impacting all workloads running on those nodes.
migrationSteps: Plan and schedule an upgrade of the container runtime on all nodes to containerd 2.0 or later.
Update the kubelet CRI configuration (or systemd service) to point to the new containerd binary and socket path if changed.
Verify that the new containerd version is compatible with your Kubernetes version and any runtime extensions.
Perform a rolling upgrade of nodes, monitoring pod health and logs for any compatibility issues.
Remove legacy containerd 1.x binaries and configuration after successful migration.
